title: Why Do We Need Leap Years?

thumbnail.plane: a shocked man in 18th-century clothes staring at a wall calendar with wide eyes and mouth open, candlelit room, cinematic close-up, dramatic rim light
thumbnail.zoom: an old paper calendar page torn in half with days missing, dark background

shots.vo: In September 1752, millions of people in Britain went to bed on the second, and woke up on the fourteenth.
shots.prompt: a sleeping family in an 18th-century English bedroom by candlelight, moonlight through the window, oil painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Eleven days. Gone. By law.
shots.prompt: an old wall calendar with pages torn away and scattered on a wooden floor, dramatic shadows
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: And it all comes back to one strange day that shows up every four years. Almost.
shots.prompt: a single calendar page curling in soft window light on an old desk, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: We think a year is 365 days. It isn't.
shots.prompt: the Earth orbiting the sun seen from space, a faint glowing orbit line, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: From one spring to the next, the Earth takes about 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes.
shots.prompt: cherry blossoms blooming on a tree in early spring, soft morning light, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Almost a quarter of a day, left over. Every single year.
shots.prompt: an antique pocket watch lying open on a stone surface, warm light, macro
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Ignore it, and the calendar slowly slides away from the seasons. In about 750 years, July would land in the middle of winter.
Ancient Rome had exactly this problem. Its calendar was so far off that festivals for the harvest fell in the wrong season.
shots.prompt: a Roman harvest festival in a snowy forum, confused citizens in togas, oil painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: So in 46 BC, Julius Caesar, advised by the astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria, fixed it.
shots.prompt: Julius Caesar in a marble hall studying a scroll with an astronomer pointing at a bronze sky globe, oil painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: To catch up, that one year ran for 445 days. Romans called it the year of confusion.
shots.prompt: a long Roman scroll unrolling across a table with endless rows of marks, lamplight
shots.negative: letters, words, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Then a simple rule. Three years of 365 days, and every fourth year, one extra day. The leap year was born.
shots.prompt: a stone Roman calendar carved into a wall, lit by torches, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, words, logo, watermark

shots.vo: But Caesar's year was 365 and a quarter days. Too long, by about eleven minutes.
shots.prompt: a sundial casting a long shadow at sunset in an ancient courtyard, cinematic
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Eleven minutes a year sounds like nothing. Over sixteen centuries, it added up to ten whole days.
shots.prompt: a medieval monk tracking dates in a huge book by candlelight, stacks of old calendars around him
shots.negative: letters, words, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Easter, tied to the spring equinox, was drifting out of place.
shots.prompt: a grand cathedral at dawn in spring, golden light on the facade, wide view
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: In 1582, Pope Gregory the Thirteenth deleted the extra days. In Catholic countries, Thursday the 4th of October was followed by Friday the 15th.
shots.prompt: a Renaissance pope signing a parchment decree at a desk in the Vatican, cardinals watching, oil painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, logo, watermark

shots.vo: And he changed the rule. Century years are not leap years, unless they divide by 400.
That's why 1900 had no February 29th, but 2000 did.
shots.prompt: fireworks over a city skyline on a millennium New Year's night, crowds celebrating, wide view
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Protestant Britain refused a pope's calendar. For 170 years. By 1752 it was eleven days behind, so eleven days had to go.
shots.prompt: the British Parliament in the 1750s, lords in wigs debating in a wood-panelled chamber, oil painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Legend says angry crowds marched shouting give us our eleven days. Historians have found almost no proof it ever happened.
shots.prompt: a crowd in 18th-century London street at night holding torches, painting style
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: Russia waited until 1918. That's why the October Revolution actually happened in November.
shots.prompt: a snowy Saint Petersburg street in 1917 with soldiers and red banners, cinematic, desaturated
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: The calendar on your phone still runs on Gregory's rule. And it is still off. By about 27 seconds a year.
shots.prompt: a smartphone calendar glowing on a nightstand in a dark bedroom, close-up
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: That's one day in about three thousand years. Someone, someday, will have to fix it again.
shots.prompt: a futuristic city at sunrise far in the future, gleaming towers, wide view
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark

shots.vo: A leftover quarter of a day, an emperor, a pope and eleven missing days. That's the hidden why.
shots.prompt: an hourglass with the last grains of sand falling, dark background, warm light
shots.negative: text, letters, words, numbers, logo, watermark
